correctness.rationale: The paired sequence is exactly the Hausdorff moment sequence of the weighted square-pushforward of the reversible spectral measure. Radon-Nikodym splitting on the positive and negative square roots gives every inverse measure, with the residual normalization mass forced to -1. Pointwise minimization proves the compatibility criterion, and the strict excess formula on (0,1) proves uniqueness. An exact finite-state example and rational checker verify the nonidentifiability and variance consequences.

Berg--Song prove that the full autocovariance is a [-1,1]-moment sequence and the paired sequence a [0,1]-moment sequence.
The closest sharp two-lag theorem assumes nonnegative spectrum and explicitly notes that general reversible chains with negative spectrum are outside its stated envelope.

originality.rationale: The primary modern full text establishes the forward gamma and paired-Gamma moment representations and notes that the paired sequence is inadequate for the entire autocovariance sequence, but it does not give the inverse fiber, compatibility test, or exact aliasing example. The closest published positive-spectrum theorem is injective by construction and excludes negative spectrum. Targeted searches did not locate a stronger inverse-identification theorem.
residual_risks: Older operator-theoretic or moment-problem literature may contain an equivalent inverse square/sign transform under terminology unrelated to MCMC paired autocovariances.
The 1992 Geyer article was not materially readable in the available extracted PDF and therefore was not used for a noncoverage claim.
For non-finitely-supported fibers the theorem classifies spectral probability measures but does not assert finite-state Markov realizability of every fiber point.

value.rationale: The paired Gamma sequence is a standard reversible-MCMC variance object. The theorem gives a complete answer to its information content: an exact inverse fiber, a sharp uniqueness criterion, and an aperiodic finite-state witness showing that the ambiguity affects finite-horizon variance even when asymptotic variance is identical. This is a structural identifiability result rather than a routine numerical refinement.
